m They begin prayer with such a reverend compellation, as suited best to the matter of their prayer and praises; whether by Lord they meant their Saviour, who was usually so called by them, or God the Father (because the word here is not [illegible], but [illegible]) is not material; for when any person in the Trinity is invoked, the other are included; for we worship the Trinity in Vnity, and the Vnity in Trinity.

n The Creation and Government of the World, is a good consideration to confirm us under all things that befall us here.

entries.title: Acts 4:25
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
o Through the Holy Ghost by the mouth of David; so 'tis read in many ancient copies; and shews, that what David and other holy men spake, was from the Holy Ghost, and is to be attended unto, and believed as spoken by him.

p Servant or Son; Davids relation to God, is mentioned as a greater dignity than his being ruler over so great a people.

q Shews the unreasonable fury wherewith the enemies of God persecute his people

r without cause, but what themselves imagine or make, and in the event failing of their end; for all things work for the good of them that love God, Rom. 8.28. And the blood of Martyrs have been found to be the seed of the Church. These words are quoted out of Psal. 2.1.

entries.title: Acts 4:26
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s Not onely such who in a strict sense we call Kings, but any chief Governors, as Herod and Pilate were.

t The Sanhedrim or great Counsel of the Iews.

u God looks upon it as done against him, whatsoever is done against them that fear him; thus the Israelites are said to be gathered together against the Lord, Numb. 16.11. who were gathered against Moses and Aaron.

u Our Saviour was at the right hand of his Father; but they who afflict his members, afflict him; he cries from Heaven to Saul, Why persecutest thou me? Chap. 9.4. and had before told his Disciples, Luke 10.16 He that despiseth you, despiseth me.

These words do not vary in sense from what we read, Psal. 2.2. but are the same for substance.

entries.title: Acts 4:27
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Mat. 26.3. Luke 23.18.

x It speaks Christs dearness to God as a Child, and obeying of God as a Servant.

y To be a King, Priest, and Prophet to his Church.

z A strange agreement against Christ, his truths and people, (Gentiles and Iews never combin'd so together.) Henceforth it is no dishonour to any, if they follow that which is good, to have great and many enemies, for so had our Saviour; nor is it any honour to any, to persecute and despise such; so did Herod, Pilate, Iudas, &c.

entries.title: Acts 4:28
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a The Apostles mind not so much second causes, in what our Saviour or themselves suffered, but see and acknowledg God in all; who makes a streight line with a crooked stick; and is Holy, Wise and Good in over-ruling, and permitting the greatest evils, and does deserve to have praise for all things, Ephes. 5.20. see Chap. 2.23.

⸫ Thy Power and right to dispose of all persons and things; alluding to Levit. 16.8. as the lot cast for the two goats, (the disposing of which being from the Lord, Prov. 16.33.) did determine, whether of the goats should be Sacrificed, and whether should escape; so it was not without a Divine disposition, that Christ was made a sin-offering for us; tho this no way excuse the wicked instruments of his death and suffering.

entries.title: Acts 4:29
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
b They had acknowledged God the maker of Heaven, ver. 24. and accordingly here they desire, that from Heaven his dwelling place, he would behold them and their sufferings; as all things are visible to such as sit above us.

c Freeness, or presence of mind, here translated boldness, which in a good cause (for Christ and his truth) is (as all good gifts) from the Father of lights, Iames 1.17. and our Saviour hath promised that it shall be given unto us in that hour what to say, Luke 12.11, 12.

entries.title: Acts 4:30
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d They desire nothing else to embolden them, but Gods owning them and their work.

e Miracles were then necessary, as being the seal of their Commission from God; they desire to have this Patent with them, to shew as often as occasion served. By the Power and Authority of Christ; for Christ alone they sought to advance and magnifie, and not themselves by all the wonders they wrought.

entries.title: Acts 4:31
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Chap. 2.24. and 16.26.

f Miraculously moved up and down on the waves of the Sea, to evidence Gods presence with them, and acceptance of them and their prayers in an extraordinary manner.

g According to their conditions, whether Apostles (for whom these prayers were especia[illegible]ly made) or private believers.

h This was the grace they asked, ver. 29. God gave it them, and with it all other graces necessary for them; In their difficulties and wants, the greatest and holiest in the Church of God, must go to God to be supplied, and prayer is the most successful means.

entries.title: Acts 4:32
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
i As if one heart and one soul, had moved that multitude; to be sure there was one spirit in them all, that is, the Spirit of God, by whose grace they agreed in all truths, and in hearty affections towards one another.

1 Pet. 3.8.

Chap. 2.44.

k Insomuch, they were as willing, that what they had might be injoyed by their necessitous brethren, as by themselves: The community of goods was not commanded, but left at liberty, and was chosen as most expedient at such a time in that place; that it was not even then commanded, we may see Chap. 5.4. neither was it practised any where but at Ierusalem; and the rather it was practised there, that believers might shew what credit they gave to our Saviours prediction concerning the destruction of that place; in which they did not care to have or retain any thing. There might be something too to command this practice of the Church in that season: The whole Church upon the matter being in Ierusalem, and consisting of such as lived a far off, and were by persecution to be driven suddenly farther; had not such a means been yielded to, it must have perished without a miracle.

entries.title: Acts 4:33
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l By sundry miracles which they wrought, as also by their boldness with which they spake; it being no small wonder to see and hear such illeterate men testifying the truths of the [illegible]ospel, amidst so many Learned Rabbins.

m The Resurrection was the greatest point in controversie, which being granted, all things concerning Christ and the Gospel could not be denied; and therefore here it is especially mentioned.

Chap. 2.47.

n Favour and acceptation; men could not but think well of their Doctrine and ways, whom they saw so Innocent and Holy, Meek and Good, especially Gods Grace was manifest in their words and actions.

entries.title: Acts 4:34
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: o So far forth as might relieve the present necessities of believers; not that every one parted with all he had, for that had taken away (at least) the use and force of the eighth commandment, as Chap. 2.44. (for where there is no propriety, there can be no theft) now Christ came not to dissolve any Law, but to fulfil it; the meaning then is, that these early Christians, would not onely part with their revenue, but rather than their brethren should want, they would, and did [illegible]ell their free-simple.

entries.title: Acts 4:35
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
p Submitted them to the Apostles disposal; this metaphor is used 1 Cor. 15.27. He hath put all things under his feet.

q The poor mans want, is the fittest measure for our relief.

entries.title: Acts 4:36
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r Some read Ioseph; the Hebrew names when turned into Greek, meet with divers terminations or endings.

s Full of Consolation; not onely in that he gave so liberally towards the relief of the poor, parting with his possessions for them; but that he excelled in propounding inward and Spiritual comfort unto poor and rich; being of a mild disposition, and fitted to handle gently such wounds as the terrors of the Law had made.

t Tho a Levite, he might have Land, either in right of his Wife, or given to him and his Ancestors; as we read was to Phineas, Iosh. 24. ult. otherwise the Lord was the Levites portion in an especially manner.

u The Iews being dispersed all over the known World; some dwelt in Cyprus, as Ioses's parents, Sauls's parents dwelt at Tarsus, tho at this time both Saul and Ioses dwell in Ierusalem.

entries.title: Acts 4:37
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
x This is an instance of what was said, ver. 34, 35. and Ioses probably is instanced in it, either because he sold a greater quantity of Land, as having large possessions; or as being one of the first that was remarkable in this kind of charity.

y vid. ver. 35.

entries.title: Acts 5:2
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c When they had vowed the whole to God and his service, which made it a robbing of God; whatsoever pretence they might possibly have, of detaining some part for their own necessities in old age, or time of sickness; arguing a great distrust in that God, whom, when they had made their vow, they pretended to give themselves and their substance unto.

d Her subjection to her husband, not excusing her partaking in his sin and punishment.

e Their ambition carried them thus far; they would seem devout, charitable, &c. and their covetousness hindred them from going further,

f vid. Chap. 4.35.

entries.title: Acts 5:3
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
g Peter knew this deceit by the inspiration of the holy Ghost; it being most probably, not otherwise likely ever to be discovered.

h As when the heart is filled with hot spirits, it is daring and bold so when Satan filled their heart, these wretches venture upon desperate courses, and provoking sins.

Or, To deceive.

i This sin is said to be lying to the Holy Ghost, because against their own consciences, and the Spirit of God too witnessing with their spirits, Rom. 9.1. As also 2dly. because they pretended to holiness, and the service of God, when they intended onely to serve their own turns; now the Spirit is in a peculiar manner the Spirit of holiness, and the author of it in us; whom they pretended to have been moved by, but falsly. And lastly, defrauding the poor members of Christ of their right; (for so by their vow it became to be) they lyed to the holy Ghost, who constitutes and establishes the Church, and accepteth these gifts as given to God, and not to men.

entries.title: Acts 5:4
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
k A sufficient argument, that there was no command (even then) to necessitate them to part with their Estates; but onely what the present and eminent necessity of the Church did perswade them voluntarily unto.

l The doubling of this expostulation, makes the conviction the more forcible.

m As a Steward under God, to do what thou wouldest with it according to his Will; and none are, or can be otherwise disposers of what they possess.

n It seems hence, that it was a deliberate, and propensed iniquity.

o In that lying unto God is so often charged, and not express mention is made of Ananias's vow; some excuse him of Sacriledge, and charge him the deeplier with Ambition, Covetousness, Lying, and Hypocrisie, to the Apostles, whom he intended to deceive.

entries.title: Acts 5:5
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
p Exspired, and dyed. Some instances of Gods extraordinary Judgments upon sinners, were in the beginning of the Iewish Church; as upon the man that gathered sticks on the Sabbath-day, Numb. 15.35. and upon Nadab and Abihu, Levit. 10.1. And so here in the beginning of the Christian Church, to be as marks to teach us to shun such sins, and to teach us, that the God with whom we have to do, is greatly to be feared; and this miraculous way of punishing notorious sinners in the Church, was accommodated to such a time, in which Magistrates were so far from defending the Church, that they themselves were the greatest enemies unto it.

q Let others also hear, and fear, and do so no more.

entries.title: Acts 5:6
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r Such as were present at that time, and fittest for that imploy;

s according as they were wont to do to such as they intnded to prepare for Sepulture. Read what was done to the body of our Saviour, Mark 15.46.

entries.title: Acts 5:7
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
t This circumstance is expressed to confirm the truth of this History:

u not suspecting any such thing, she was the less inquisitive; and such a consternation and dread was upon all that were there, that they durst not tell her, lest they should offend Peter; as also probably, lest they should with so sudden and sad news grieve her.

x Into the Church or place, where they were met together.

entries.title: Acts 5:8
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
y An ordinary Hebraism, by which one that speaketh, first is said to answer, if it be tending towards any discourse especially.

z The certain price is not mentioned, as not being necessary to the intent of the Holy Ghost in this narrative; but be it more or less, it was the same which her husband had said the land was sold for.

a She had agreed with her husband what to say; and one sin draws on another, till it ends in perdition.

entries.title: Acts 5:9
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
b This expression of tempting God, or the Spirit of God, is not used amongst prophane Writers; and this sin is not (at lest to such a degree) committed amongst Pagans and Heathens, and is to be dreaded by all that profess the Gospel. As often as men sin against their conscience, and their consciences condemn them in what they do, so often they dare, tempt, or try, whether God be Omniscient, and knows of, or Holy, and Powerful, and will punish their sins; which they find at last to their cost.

c This the Apostle foretells ere it came to pass; the more to confirm his Authority and the truth of the Gospel.

d After thou art dead, to thy burial.

entries.title: Acts 5:10
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: e The same sins meet with the same punishment; God is no respector of Persons, Iew or Gentile, Male or Female.

entries.title: Acts 5:11
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f Thus upon the smiting of so many men in and about Beth-shemeth, 1 Sam. 6.20. They wisely demand, who is able to stand before this holy Lord God; and upon the s[illegible]aying of Vzzah, 2 Sam. 6.9. David was afraid of the Lord, Discite justitiam moniti.

g Out of the pale of the Church, Gods judgments do restrain in a great measure wicked men.

entries.title: Acts 5:12
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Chap. 2.43.

h By the Apostles Ministry; tho they were holy and excellent men, they were but instruments; the power they acted by, was Gods; which also they had prayed for, and acknowledged, Chap. 4.30.

i Generally among the meaner sort, according to that question, have any of the Rul[illegible]rs believed on him? Iohn 7.48. Not many mighty, not many noble are called, 1 Cor. 1.26.

k A large and capacious place, where they might with greatest convenience hear, and see what was done and said.

Chap 3 11.

entries.title: Acts 5:13
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l Such who were not of the common sort of people, and here seem to be distinguished from them; or of the rest, (more largely) who had not joyned themselves to the Church, being amazed at this judgment on these two Hypocrites, durst not make a formal shew of Religion, unless they had a thorow perswasion in their mind concerning the truth of it, and a firm resolution in their conversation to live answerably unto it.

John 9 22. and 12.42. and 19.38.

entries.title: Acts 5:14
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: m This explains the former verse, and helps us against mistaking it; for this wonderful judgment was so far from being a hinderance to the truth of the Gospel, that it is turned to the furtherance of it; for tho great men, and such as were insincere, were terrified from owning Christ and his Doctrine, others did more readily imbrace them by reason of it.

entries.title: Acts 5:15
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Or, In every street.

n Into every street generally taken, it being a common practice where they came, and not in one street onely.

o These weak and unlikely means, did more shew the power to be of God, and was the greater confirmation to the truth of the Gospel; and thus was fulfilled what our Saviour had promised to the Apostles, and such as should believe in him, Iohn 14.12. that they should do greater works than he did.

entries.title: Acts 5:16
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
p The variety and grievousness of these evils, did but the more commend the power which was present with the Apostles.

Ma[illegible]. 16.17.

q An evidence, that these cures were not wrought by second causes; for the best Medicines do not always succeed; as also, in that they were perfectly and suddenly cured, who were thus miraculously cured; the God of Nature, restoring Nature, beyond what means and art could do.

entries.title: Acts 5:17
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r Moved at the report of these things, went out of the Council to observe what was done.

s There were both Pharises and Sadduces in their Sanhedrim or great Council, as appears Acts 23.6. but the High Priest and a great part, were at this time Sadduces.

t Or zeal, which is the best, when kindled (as the fire on the Altar) from Heaven, regularly acting for Gods truth and word; and the worst, when enflamed by carnal affections, and set upon wrong objects for self ends. The pick these Sadduces had against the Apostles and their Doctrine, was, because they taught the Resurrection, which the Sadduces denied.

Or, Envy.

entries.title: Acts 5:18
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: See Acts 4.3.

entries.title: Acts 5:19
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Chap. 12.7, and 16.26.

a God useth the Ministry of Angels, tho he might otherwise do what pleaseth him; An Angel rolled away the stone from the door of the Sepulchre. Angels ministred to Christ, Matth. 4.11. And are all ministring spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation, Hebr. 1.14. And encamp round about them that fear God, Psal. 34.7.

b And shut them again, after that the Apostles were gone out, as appears ver. 23.

entries.title: Acts 5:20
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c The word implies courage and stedfastness of mind, as well as such a posture of the body.

d Without preferring some acceptable truths, before others more ingrateful, it necessary towards their Salvation: Christ for a time did limit them; they might not tell any that he was Jesus the Christ, Matth. 16.20. nor the vision which they had seen in his transfiguration, Matth. 17.9. Now this prohibition is taken off. Thus the Sun does not shine in his full glory all at once.

e Some admit of an Hypailage, and joyn the pronoun to the other substantive, reading in this place, These words of life; and the rather because by this life, is ordinarily understood the present, temporary life, as in 1 Cor. 15.19. but there needs not this translatiti[illegible]us sense; by this life, the Angel might very well understand eternal life and Salvation, for that was it which the Sadduces denied, and for the Preaching of which life the Apostles were imprisoned.

entries.title: Acts 5:21
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f Having received a command from God, they resolve to obey him rather than man.

g Taking the first opportunity, tho they could not but be sensible of the danger they ran into.

i The Judges of their inferior Courts, or the chief amongst the Priests or Senators; either living in the City, or coming thither upon that festival occasion.

k The San[illegible]edrim or great Council.

entries.title: Acts 5:22
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: k These men, thus sent to hinder the spreading of the Gospel, could not be a means of confirming it, when they saw and declared what they found; so easily can God make use of what is intended against his truth and people, unto the advantage of either.

entries.title: Acts 5:23
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: l All means imaginable were used to secure their prisoners; but when God will deliver, what can keep them? when God will work, who can hinder? Iob 11.10. It is strange, that so great evidence of the innocency of the Apostles, and truth of their Doctrine, should be ineffectual; but prejudice is insuperable, unless to the mighty Power of the grace of God, and this boldness cannot be cured, but by Gods Ephphat ha

entries.title: Acts 5:24
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Luke 22.4.

m The Commander over the Soldiers, who were set to guard the Temple, either to secure the treasure there, or to be in a readiness to suppress any tumult thereabouts; Pilate speaks of this, Matth. 27.65.

n The heads of the Families, or chief of the courses of the Priests.

o By what means these wonderful things were done; for they were loath to see and acknowledge God in them.

entries.title: Acts 5:25
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: p So true is that in Isaiah 8 10. Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; but the counsel of the Lord standeth for ever. Psal. 33.11.

entries.title: Acts 5:26
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
q They might peradventure, think it needless or impossible, to bind them against their wills, who had opened the prison, and so miraculously came out; howsoever another more certain reason is given of it: They feared men more than God, who had done so great things amongst them.

Mat. 21.26. Chap. 4.21.

entries.title: Acts 5:27
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: r When they are about to do the greatest injuries, they pretend to right; and will not judge them, without giving them leave to answer for themselves.

entries.title: Acts 5:28
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s As indeed they had, Acts 4.18. hence they aggravated the Apostles crime as done out of malice, and not out of ignorance.

t This Name, and this mans blood, are odious reflections, full of con[illegible]umely against our blessed Saviour; as if he had not been worthy the naming by them.

u They shunned not the sin of murder, but are afraid or ashamed of the imputation of it; as many scruple not to commir that wickedness, which they would be loath to be thought guilty of.

x The punishment of his blood-shedding.

entries.title: Acts 5:29
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: y This they all agree in; and it is the common sense of all considering men. As Socrates in his Apology told the Athenians; I imbrace and love you, O Athenians, and yet I will obey God rather than you; this the Apostles had formerly asserted, Chap. 4.19.

entries.title: Acts 5:30
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Cha. 3.13, 15.

z This is the rather mentioned by the Apostle, that they might not think our Saviour, or they his Ministers, Preached any other God unto them, but him whom they had worshipped from their fore-fathers.

Chap. 10.39. and 13.29. 1 Pet. 2.24.

a A tree, or wood, which is rather mentioned than a Cross, that the allusion to Deut. 21.23. might be more full; where he that is hanged on a tree is accursed; and in that Christ was made a curse for us, Gal. 3.13.

entries.title: Acts 5:31
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Heb. 2.10. See Luke 24.46, 47.

b See Chap. 2.33.

c To conquer and subdue all his enemies, to defend and protect his subjects.

d To save from sin according to his name Jesus, Matth. 1.21. viz. from the condemnation that is due unto it, and the pollution that is required by it; repentance is the gift of God; and nothing does more avail with us to repent, than the loss of Christ, (his bitter suffering and death) by whom the world is crucified unto us, Gal. 6.14. and if repentance includes newness of life, (as it does) who would not walk in that way which our blessed Lord hath recommended, and in which onely we can injoy him? that doing as he did, we may come at last to be where he is,

f which never fails to accompany true repentance; and is therefore also called repentance unto life, Chap. 11.18.

entries.title: Acts 5:32
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Joh. [illegible].26, 27.

g They refuse not to [illegible]ear their testimony for Christ, who witnessed a good profession for us.

h The holy Ghost does witness, 1. By the Apostles, through his grace and strength they bear their record. 2. By all the miracles that were wrought, for they were onely done by his Power. 3. By enabling any to believe these things, which belief is his work. 4. Not to say that the holy Ghost was a witness of the things concerning Christ at his Baptism, and the several attestations he gave, saying, This is my beloved So[illegible], Matth. 3.17.

Chap. 2.4.

c Some read, believe in him, which is to the same purpose; for there is no true repentance where there is no faith: nor no saving faith, where there is no repentance and amendment.

entries.title: Acts 5:33
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Chap. 7.54.

k They grinned with their teeth, visibly shewing the rage and fury that was within them, by which they were as sawn and divided asunder; malice and rage being a grievous torment to the cruel and malicious, [illegible].

entries.title: Acts 5:34
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l This Sect was accounted more mild than the Sadduces.

m 'Tis thought that this man was the same, at whose feet Paul sate, Chap. 22.3. that he was the instructor to Barnabas and St. Stephen, with many other stories concerning him are doubtful; howsoever God made use of him, tho as yet an enemy to his Church and people, to plead for, and protect them to his Power; God can effect any thing without, or against means, and suddenly to make such as were against him, to be for him and his truth.

n That they might consult amongst themselves what to do with them: thus Chap. 4.[illegible]5.

entries.title: Acts 5:35
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: o A wise and good caution; for he that injures another, brings the worse mischief upon himself; both in the sense of having done evil, and in being exposed to the revengeing hand of God, whose property vengeance is, Hebr. 10.30.

entries.title: Acts 5:36
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
p Probably under the reign of Augustus, as he whom Iosephus mentions, was another under the reign of Claudius.

q Some suppose it a contracted name of Theodorus, as Demas is thought to be of Demetrius; tho others think it to be of an Hebrew original.

Or, Believed.

entries.title: Acts 5:37
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r Whether this was the same Iudas, who was called Gaulonite, from the place of his birth, a Town in or near Galilee; and Galileus from the Province its self in which he was born, it is not so material to discuss Iosephus makes mention of two of this name.

s Setting down all their names at the command of the Roman Emperor, whereby, 1 They professed themselves to be his subjects. 2. They payed him a certain rate, in token of subjection, for every head, as Poll[illegible] money. 3. By this means he knew the number of his subjects, and the strength or weakness of every Province; this was another tax than that, mentioned Luke 2.2. which is there called the first.

entries.title: Acts 5:38
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
t He undertakes to advise them what they should do in the present case.

u Have nothing to do with them, as Pilates wife advised him concerning our Saviour, Matth. 27.19. Gamaliel interposes, partly, out of his moderate and mild disposition; partly out of fear, lest if they slew the Apostles, they might incense the Romans, who were very jealous of their Authority and had taken away the power of Capital punishments from the Iews.

Prov. 21.30. Isa. 8.10. Matth. 15.13.

x This Argument, or Dilemma, which Gamaliel uses for the sparing of the Apostles, is of force either way; (as that question our Saviour propounds concerning the baptism of Iohn, Matth. 21.25.)

y This first part is evident, for that building must needs fall which is built upon the sand, Matth. 7.27.

entries.title: Acts 5:39
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
z The other part of the Dilemma, Prov. 19.21. Isaiah 46.10. The counsel of the Lord, that shall stand; and it must needs be so, for all power is his, in whom we live and move, Chap. 17.28.

Chap. 9.5. and 239.

a They who afflict, and contend with his people unjustly, tho they little think so, set themselves against God, who will overcome at the last, and triumph over his, and his peoples enemies.

entries.title: Acts 5:40
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
b They yielded to his reason and argument, being perswaded and convinced by it.

c This was what our Saviour had foretold them, Ma[illegible]th. 1[illegible].17. and thus the husbandmen took the housholders servants and beat them, Matth. 21.35. They had power yet left them by the Romans, to punish offenders in their Synagogues, but not capitally nor publickly.

d In this they left the good advice of Gamaliel, who had warned them not to fight against God.

entries.title: Acts 5:41
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
e It argued full perswasion of the truth, and great resolution to abide by it, that they could account so frail a disgrace for Christs sake, to be an honour.

Mat. 5.12. Heb. 10.34. James 1.2. 1 Pet. 4.13.

f 'Tis a condescension and favour, when God uses any to give testimony unto his truth, altho it be by their suffering, Phil. 1.29. Vnto you it is given, not onely to believe, but to suffer; as if to suffer for Christ, were as great, if not a greater gift than to believe in him.

g Scourging being a servile and disgraceful punishment.

h Christs name, or for Christs sake, to assert his truth, &c. some do not read the Pronoun, but the name put absolutely for God, as was usual amongst the Iews, out of reverence to Gods name, lest they should prophane it.

entries.title: Acts 5:42
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
i This is the same with what we read, Acts 20.20. publickly, and from house to house; that is, in the Temple, and publick places, they preached unto the Iews, and in more private places, (or houses) where they saw it needful; unto such they conversed with.

k They visited their flock, and instructed, exhorted, comforted them as their condition required: See the power of the grace of God; these we[illegible]e the men who forsook Christ, when the Souldiers came to apprehend him; they durst not be seen in his company: yet now they profess his Name, and abide by their profession, though they are derided and beaten for it.

entries.title: Acts 6:2
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
n For such was their number now again, Matthias having supplied the place of Iudas; this is that blessed number, or the root of it, which God hath so much magnified.

Exod. 18.17.

o Preaching of the word, and other duties belonging to it; either providing for the agapae and love-Feasts, or distributing to the necessities whereby they might be fed, and their tables provided.

entries.title: Acts 6:3
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Deut. 1.13. Chap. 1.21, 22. and 16.2. 1 Tim. 3.7.

p As carefully and circumspectly, as ye would in any cases of your own concerns.

q A good direction, that obbliges to this day, in all elections of any for the service of God, and his Church.

r Of the gifts and graces of the holy Ghost, which were not bestowed on the Apostles onely.

s Or prudence, and skill in the word of God, which onely is able to make a man wise unto Salvation, 2 Tim. 3.15.

entries.title: Acts 6:4
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
t We will stick close, and with perseverance, to this work.

u The two great imploys of a Minister of Jesus Christ; to pray unto God for the people, and to speak unto the people from the Lord; these, tho great businesses, they durst not delegate from themselves unto others to perform for them.

entries.title: Acts 6:5
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
x All these being Greek names, 'tis likely they were all Hellenists, and descended from Hebrew Parents, but born in forreign Countries; or amongst the Iews they might have other names, which St. Luke writing this History, translated into Greek.

Chap. 11.24.

Chap. 8.5, 26. and 21.[illegible].

y See Chap. 2.10.

entries.title: Acts 6:6
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
z Prayer is the salt, which seasoneth and sanctifieth all things.

Chap. 8.17. and 13.3. 1 Tim. 4.14. 2 Tim. 1.6.

a A rite used in the Church of old, 1. In their Sacrifices, Exod 29.15. 2. In their blessings, Gen. 48.14. 3. In their designations unto a charge or office; thus Moses on Ioshua, Numb. 27.18. and from thence it was easilier derived unto the Gospel-Church. Our Saviour blessing thus the children which were brought unto him, Matth. 19.13. and thus also were Ministers ordained in the Primitive times, 1 Tim. 5.22.

entries.title: Acts 6:7
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Chap. 12 and 19.20. Col. 1.6.

b None so violent opposers of the Gospel as these were, (their interest in all likelihood, heigthning their opposition) yet great is truth, especially the spirit of truth, and did prevail; and tho in its self, the number might not be so great, as to be called a great multitude; yet considering who they were that were converted, it was very wonderful, and the fewer might pass for a many.

c Christianity is not a bare speculation, but a practical Religion; and we believe no more than we practice, fac quod dicis & fides est. Aug.

entries.title: Acts 6:8
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d Enabled to Preach, dispute, do, and suffer all things through Christ.

e Of whom he cured many, or among the people, in that he did these wonders publickly.

entries.title: Acts 6:9
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f Synagogues were as Colledges in our Universities, being used for Instruction and Learning; and were distinguished according to the persons that frequented them.

g Some think, these were natives of a certain Countrey in Africa, from whence they were so called; but more probably, they were such as were manumitted or made free, (as the word is commonly used for such) and in a middle condition between such as were free-born, and such as were bond-slaves; and might desire to frequent with those of their own rank.

h The Iews spake of no less than 480. Synagogues at Ierusalem, a vast number, and probably increased by them, tho several places are called Cyrene; this (from whence they took their name) was in Africa in all likelihood, it being joyned with that of the Alexandrians: So God pleased to sever the Hellenists, (or Iews by traduction) for the Gentiles were not yet called; that they might all hear the Gospel in the Language they understood best.

entries.title: Acts 6:10
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Exod. 4.12. Isa. 54.17. Luke 21.15.

i They did oppose it, but ineffectually.

k The foolishness of God is wiser than men, 1 Cor. 1.25. What then is his wisdom, through which this holy man spake?

l The holy Ghost directing him, and putting a Divine Power upon what he spake, according to the promise, Matth. 10.20.

entries.title: Acts 6:11
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: m What these blasphemous words were, we have verse 14. which shew, that the vail was yet over their hearts, and that they could not indure to hear, that the shadows must flee away, when the Sun is risen, and the Types be abolished, when the substance of the things Typified is exhibited; for this truth was all the blasphemy this holy Martyr was guilty of.

entries.title: Acts 6:12
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: n Being overcome by reason and arguments, they betake themselves to all the evil arts imaginable; they suborn witnesses against St. Stephen, (as was done against Naboth) and (that we read of) never before; they make the people, and the number, (which is usually the worst) on their side; then they complain of him to the Priests, &c. and lest any, or all these, should fail, they lay violent hands on him themselves. Sin goes on as a Current, and never stops, unless an Almighty word be spoken unto it to go no further.

entries.title: Acts 6:13
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: o They mingled in their testimony, false things with truths, as they who witnessed against our Saviour had done. St. Stephen might possibly have inculcated what our Saviour had foretold, Luke 19.43. and both have been very innocent; for neither of them spake with any abhorrence of, much less blasphemy [illegible]gainst the Law or the Temple; but in that the witnesses perverted and added to their words, they are deservedly branded as false witnesses; falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus, is a granted maxime in the case of witness-bearing.

entries.title: Acts 6:14
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
p That is the Temple; Ieremy had foretold this long ago, and did escape, tho very narrowly, Ier. 26.12, 16. Daniel had Prophesied of the destruction both of the City and Sanctuary, Dan. 9.26. and yet these were in great respect amongst them; and none could speak more plainly of the calling of the Gentiles, than Malachi, Chap. 1.11. and yet when the Apostles came to apply these very things more home, and close, they could not indure them.

Or, Rites.

entries.title: Acts 6:15
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: q With an extraordinary lustre and radiancy, above what appears in men, whereby they might be distinguished, as Matth. 28.2, 3. affecting the beholders with admiration; thus Moses his face did shine.

entries.title: Acts 7:2
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
t To take away any prejudice they might have conceived against him; and to recommend, not his person so much, as his Doctrine to them; he calls them Brethren, 1. As hoping in the same promises with them. 2. Observing the same Law. 3. Worshipping the same God.

u A word of respect (especially) the elder amongst them, or his Judges: thus the Roman Senators were called Fathers, and Magistrates ought to be reverenced as the Fathers of their Countrey.

x Who is also called. Psal. 24.7. The King of glory, from whom all glory descends to Angels or Men. By this and what follows, St. Stephen would shew that he honoured the true God, and thought respectfully of the Law, the Temple, and the Patriarchs, whom he was accused to contemn and disgrace.

y He names Abraham, because he was accounted the first Father, and Patriarch of the Iews, and had the first clear promise, that the Messiah should come of his Seed.

z Mesopotamia is sometimes taken strictly for that Countrey, which lies betwixt the two Rivers, Tigris and Euphrates, from whence it had its name; sometimes more largely, including Chalde, and so 'tis taken here.

a A City of the Parthians, in the borders of Mesopotamia, towards the Land of Canaan.

entries.title: Acts 7:3
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
b This command given unto Abraham, we read of, Gen. 12.1, 5, 6. and is here the rather spoken of by St. Stephen, to prove that Abraham was in the favour of God, and did truly serve him, before he ever saw the Land of Canaan, and before the ceremonial Law was given by Moses, and much more before the Temple was built; and therefore it could not be blasphemy in him, to hold that God might be served without those ceremonies, and worshipped elsewhere than in Ierusalem.

c This was the glory of Abrahams faith, that it submitted absolutely to God, and enabled Abraham to go he knew not whither, Hebr. 11.8. for God did not so much as name the place he would have him go unto.

entries.title: Acts 7:4
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d Abraham had as great a love to his kindred and native Countrey, as others have; but he had a greater faith, which made him yield to Gods call and command, and follow from place to place the will of God, who is said here to have removed Abraham, and does chuse the Inheritance and habitation for his people, Psal. 47.4.

Gen. 11.31

entries.title: Acts 7:5
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
e 'Tis true that Abraham had a field, and the Cave of Machpelah, Gen. 23.9. but that was of no use to Abraham whilst alive, but to bury him in when dead; besides, it was not as an inheritance by Gods gift, but it was purchased with his money.

f Whereby the least parcel of ground is meant; hence St. Stephen would prove, that Abrahams happiness, and theirs too, if they rightly understood it, did not depend upon the enjoyment of that place and Countrey.

Gen. 12.7 and 13.15.

g Faith met with a double difficulty, not onely Abraham must believe he should have all that Countrey given him for an inheritance, in which he had not a foot of land, but he must also believe, that it should be his seeds after him, when as he had no children; but thus faith is the evidence of things not seen, Hebr. 11.1.

entries.title: Acts 7:6
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
h As men which dwell in houses that are not their own; which seem to contradict the promise mentioned in the foregoing verse; but it is onely to make Abraham the more believe against hope, in hope, as 'tis said, Rom. 4.18. tho there were never so many difficulties more, for what God hath promised, faith would overcome them all.

i This very space of four hundred yea[illegible], is also mentioned, Gen. 15.13, 16. Which is thus computed, from the birth of Isaac (the promised seed) to the birth of Iacob, sixty years; from Iacobs birth, to his going into Egypt, one hundred and thirty years, from thence to their deliverance out of Egypt, two hundred and ten years; this period is accounted, Exod. 12.40, 41. to be four hundred and thirty years; which also St. Paul reckons by, Gal. 3.17. but then thirty years is added unto the account, being the space of time betwixt the first promise made unto Abraham of this seed, and the birth of Isaac, in whom the promise was to be fulfilled: St. Stephen here reckoning onely from the birth of Isaac.

entries.title: Acts 7:7
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
q Or punish; and so the Egyptians were punished, not by humane means, but by Divine power, and with Gods own immediate hand, and that in the fulness of time, the very night in which Gods promise was to take effect: and therefore 'tis a night to be much observed, Exod. 12.42. as shewing, that the Sabbath of his people, and the destruction of his enemies slumber not, 2 Pet. 2.3.

Exod. [illegible].12.

r In Mount Horeb. The reason why God delivers his people is, that they may serve him, as Luke 1.74, 75. and so long as God hath any work for them to do in this World, he will preserve and deliver them.

entries.title: Acts 7:8
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Gen. 17.9, 10.

s Abraham, of whom he was speaking.

t Of which Covenant, Circumcision was the sign and seal, by which on the part of Abraham and his seed, it was stipulated, that they should put off all carnal affections,

Gen. 21.2, 3, 4.

u after the promise: so that the promises were not given for Isaacs sake; but Isaac was given for the promise sake: which made these things more fit to represent Gospel grace, which St. Stephen was Preaching of.

Gen. 25.26.

Gen. 29.31, &c. and 30.5. and 35.23.

x The heads of the Tribes, from whom they were denominated. Of this Genealogy, see Matth. 1.1, 2, &c. and the History of it in Genesis.

entries.title: Acts 7:9
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Gen. 37.4, 28. Psal. 105.17.

y Enraged; the holy Martyr accommodates his apology so, as that they may ye[illegible] have occasion to reflect on themselves:

z for as they had sold our Saviour unto strangers, so had their Fathers sold Ioseph.

r To favour, and bless him; for Gods presence brings all good along with it: with this he comforts himself and others; that it was not without example or precedent that God should be with such whom their persecutors could not endure.

entries.title: Acts 7:10
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
b The effect of Gods presence with him, which to his people is always in an especial manner, not onely as he is with all other Creatures; but as the Soul is with the Body, most effectually, so is God with them.

Gen. 41.37.

c Thus God brought Daniel into favour, Dan. 1.9. and hath all hearts in his hands.

entries.title: Acts 7:11
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d This is mentioned, Gen. 41.54, &c.

e As seldome any mischief comes alone: Rapine, and many diseases follow Famine.

f Any course dyet, grass or herbs.

entries.title: Acts 7:12
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
g The history is known, Gen 42.1.

h Our Progenitors, Iacobs Sons, from whom we are descended.

entries.title: Acts 7:13
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
i Upon their second coming into Egypt, Gen. 45.3, 4, 16. Ioseph made himself known unto them.

k For the continuance of their sustenance, and fulfilling of what was foretold.

entries.title: Acts 7:14
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Deut. 10.22.

l His affinity, and not consanguinity onely, which may be the reason why, tho in Gen. 46.26. it is said, that all the souls that came with Iacob into Egypt, were sixty six. (it being then added, they were all such as came out of his loyns) yet it is said they were seventy persons, Gen. 46.27. Iacob, Ioseph, and Iosephs two sons (who were also of the promised seed) being added unto the number. In this account of St. Stephen, his Sons wives might be added, which make up seventy five. [illegible]here are other accounts of this difference; but it is not of any consequence as to faith and holy living, which are onely necessary unto Salvation: the wonderful increase to so many hundred thousands of men, besides children, spoken of Exod. 12.37. notwithstanding the barbarous cruelty of the Egyptians, is to be admired.

m The nobler and better part by which they are numbred, and according unto which they are esteemed by God.

entries.title: Acts 7:15
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Gen. 46.[illegible]

n Which St. Stephen puts them in mind of, the rather that he might insinuate, No Countrey, nor Place, nor Temple were so necessary, but that notwithstanding (they had none of them) their fore-fathers did live and die in the fear and favour of God, altho in Egypt, out of the promised Land, &c.

Gen. 49.[illegible]

entries.title: Acts 7:16
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Exod. 13 [illegible] Josh. 24 3[illegible]

o That they carried Ioseph to bury him in Canaan, according to the oath he made them take, Gen 50.25. i[illegible] certain, and that this was desired to be done for him out of faith, Hebr. 11.22. but it is not so certain, (unless this pl[illegible]ce be so [illegible]nderstood) that the rest of the Patriarchs were so translated after their death: yet it is very likely; fo[illegible] first, they had as much reason to desire it, as Ioseph h[illegible]d; they believed the same promises, and had an interest in that Land as well as he. Secondly, Their posterity bare the same respect unto them, that Iosephs Family did to him. Thirdly, It seems alike reasonable, that none of those twelve Heirs to the Land of Canaan, should be left in the Land of bondage.

Gen. 23.[illegible] and 33.19.

p This place is acknowledged to be most difficult, and the difficulties are better not to be mentioned, than ill solved; which the nature of these notes (not to mention other reasons) might occasion: whosoever will consider the intended shortness of the story, with the usual Idioms of the Hebrew Language, from which it was deduced, may take this as a Paraphrase upon the whole Verse: And Iacob, and our fathers died, and were removed to Sichem, and were laid in Sepulchres, in that which Abraham bought for money, and in that that was bought for the Sons of Emor, the Father of Sichem. Dr. Lightfoot, in locum.

entries.title: Acts 7:17
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
q Of the fulfilling of the promise; either of the increase of his seed, or of their deliverance out of Bondage, for both were promised, Gen 22.17. tho at that very time there were the greatest endeavours to hinder either, when God accomplished both.

Exo. 1.7, [illegible] Psal. 10[illegible].2[illegible]

entries.title: Acts 7:18
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: r These words, are taken from the Septuagint, Exod. 1.8.

entries.title: Acts 7:19
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s Pharaoh resolves to deal (as he thought) wisely, Exod. 1.10. and 'tis acknowledged, that the Egyptians dealt subtilly with them, Psal. 105.25. For they do not at once destroy them, which might have been hazardous, (the Israelites being so numerous) neither could Egypt well spare at once so many Inhabitants; (too great and sudden evacuations, cause swoonings) but they endeavour their ruine by degrees, 1. Wasting them by hard labours. 2. Commanding the Midwifes privately to kill their Males. 3.

Exod. 1.2[illegible]

t Casting out, or exposing any whom they found spared. Yet this people, attempted upon by so many secret and open means to bring them to destruction, God did preserve, and so he will his Church, (which they did typifie) ma[illegible]gre all the endeavours, the most potent malice can use against it.

entries.title: Acts 7:20
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Exod. 2[illegible] [illegible]

Hebr. 11.[illegible]

Heb. [illegible] God.

a Or fair to God; which tho some understand of the inward beauty of the mind, (which is indeed the most admirable) yet in this place there is no more to be understood by it, than the wonderful beauty of his Body, which God bestowed in an extraordinary measure upon him, that it might be a means to attract the care and pity of Pharaoh's Daughter, as it afterwards came to pass; besides, that which is eminent in any kind, is by an Hebraism said to be of God; upon this account Niniveh is called a City of God, Ionah 3.3. And we read of Rachels great wrestlings, or wrestlings of God, Gen. 3.8. Iosephus says, That Moses was so beautiful, that all who passed by, left their business they were about, to gaze at him. Antiq. 2.5.

entries.title: Acts 7:21
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
x Exposed and left, Exod. 2.2. &c. now was the time for God to take him up, as in Psal. 27.10.

y An enemy to Gods Israel; yet God did make use of her to bring up, and educate Moses who was their deliverer.

z Adopting him for her Son, Exod. 2.10. and giving him Education accordingly.

entries.title: Acts 7:22
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
a The Egyptians were anciently famous for Learning, especially in Astronomy, and some other parts of Philosophy.

b He was Eloquent.

c His deeds were equal to his words: He could do as well as say, what became him.

entries.title: Acts 7:23
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
[illegible]. 2.11.

c This Age of Moses is not set down in his History; but they might have it by tradition, which is here confirmed unto us by the Holy Pen-man: these fourty years Moses spent in Pharaohs Court.

d It speaks these thoughts and resolutions to have been from God, that such a great Courtier should so far debase himself; therefore this is deservedly attributed unto his Faith, Hebr. 11.25. which is the gift of God, Eph. 2 8.

entries.title: Acts 7:24
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: e This fact of Moses some defend by the Law of Nature, which allows us to protect the innocent; but many things we know were done by an extraordinary warrant, which we are not to imitate; nor by our own Authority to avenge our selves or others.

entries.title: Acts 7:25
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Or, Now.

f This they might have inferred, 1. From his extraordinary deliverance out of the Egyptians hands, and out of the River when young. 2. From his readiness to defend them, ('twas wonderful, that such an one as he was, and might have been, should mind them.) 3. From the drawing near of the time of their deliverance, which they could not without negligence be wholly ignorant of.

g By his means and Ministry.

h Stupidity is frequently charged upon this people: They then did not receive Moses, as these now would not receive Christ.

entries.title: Acts 7:26
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
i As one appointed by God to deliver them, which he had evidenced before.

k With great earnestness, and as far as words could do, he compelled them.

l These words are not mentioned, Exod. 2.13. but something otherwise than here; but the sense is here and there the same.

m Brethren, not so much being all descended from Abraham and the Patriarchs; but in that they all worshipped one and the same God, which is the greatest obligation to concord and agreement that can be; and if any offence be given, or trespass committed, it obliges us as much to pass it by and pardon it: Forgive the trespass of the servants of the God of thy father, Gen. 50.17.

entries.title: Acts 7:27
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
n The injurious are most averse from peace, and one sin makes way for another.

[illegible] Chap. [illegible]

o This was a causless cavil, especially from such an one as had known what Moses had done, as an essay of his being the deliverer of Gods Israel.

entries.title: Acts 7:28
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: p He charges this great crime upon Moses, to hinder him from further reproving of him; tho recrimination do not make him, or any other more innocent; yet men ordinarily use it, as if it were some satisfaction to them, that they are not wicked alone; but that others are as bad or worse; this better befits an Egyptian than an Israelite.

entries.title: Acts 7:29
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
q Knowing that what he had done to the Egyptian, would be discovered to Pharaoh, and his life in danger.

r Inhabited by the posterity of Madian Abrahams Son, by Keturah, Gen. 25.1, 2. Moses was fourty years in Egypt, fourty years in Madian, with Iethro or Iether, who was called also Revel, Exod. 2.18. and Hobah, Numb. 10.29. and the other fourty years in the wilderness, which make up the hundred and twenty years of his life, Deutr. 34.7. This makes to St. Stephens purpose, to prove that God is always with them that fear him, in what Countrey or place soever; as he was with Abraham in Mesopotamia, and with his people in Egypt, so with Moses in Madian.

entries.title: Acts 7:30
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s So long it pleased God to try Moses his faith, and his peoples patience:

t to the Desert of Arabia, where the Law was afterwards delivered, Exod. 18.5. and 19: 3.

u Not a Created, but the Increated Angel, the Angel of the New-Covenant, as may be seen ver. 32. and by Moses putting off his shoes because the place was holy, Exod. 3.2, 5. he is also in the four first verses of that Chapter, called the Lord.

x God still appeared in such a manner as was most instructive to them he appeared to, and to us; as here in a flame of fire in a bush, to shew that he was with his people in all their sufferings, and would so provide, that they should not be consumed by them; they might be purified, but should not be destroyed.

entries.title: Acts 7:31
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content: y Seeing the bush on a flame, and not consumed; contrary to the nature of devouring flames, [illegible]hat he might be convinced of Gods presence; and made the more attentive to what God should say, and prepared to yield obedience unto it.

entries.title: Acts 7:32
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Mat. 22.32. Heb. 11.16.

z That he might know from whom he had his Commission, and by whom he was to be sent.

a Mention is made of these, because God had made unto them the promise of delivering their posterity, which he was now about to do, the time being fully come.

b All great admiration hath some fear joyned with it; Gods appearing, tho in mercy, was ever full of terror and amazement; what will his appearing be, when he shall come in Judgment to render vengeance? who then shall be able to abide?

entries.title: Acts 7:33
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
c Either out of reverence to the Divine presence, as Iosh. 5: 15. or that thereby he might shew that he resigned himself wholly to Gods will and disposal; as in Ruth 4.7. The kinsman by pulling off his shoe and giving it to Boaz, did resign all his right he might have had to Ruth and the inheritance.

d Whilest God manifested his presence there.

entries.title: Acts 7:34
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
e Seeing I have seen, I have attentively seen and considered; It is doubled for to shew the certainty of it; if earthly parents, especially look after their Children when weak, much more our Heavenly Father.

g Spoken after the manner of men, according unto which God is said to come down unto any, when he delivers them from their troubles; and to go from them, when he leaves them in them, see Exod. 3.7, 8. from which place according to the reading of the Septuagint, these words are taken.

f Tho but sighs, and scarce framed into words.

entries.title: Acts 7:35
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
h Or a Redeemer; but onely as a Type of Christ, in whom alone we have redemption through his blood, Eph. 1.7. As Moses by the blood of the Paschal Lamb, brought forth, and saved the people of Israel.

i The power of the Angel; it was not Moses, but God that wrought so great Salvation.

entries.title: Acts 7:36
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Exod. 7. & 8. & 9. & 10. & 11. & 14.

k God could with the least word or motion of his Will, save his people; but he chuseth so to do his wonderful works, that they may be had in remembrance.

l 'Tis not agreed why 'tis so called; but this name of that Sea is mentioned in prophane Authors. This whole verse, as divers others, refer to the History of it in Exodus, from the beginning to the fifteenth Chapter.

Exod. 16.1.

entries.title: Acts 7:37
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
m St. Stephen would shew, that he was so far from speaking against Moses, (as they falsly imagined) that he recommended no[illegible]e but him, whom Moses had so long before spoken of.

Deu. 1[illegible].15, [illegible].

n Christ the Messiah, and head of the Prophets, See Chap. 3.22.

Or, As my self.

Mat. 17.5.

o Or obey.

entries.title: Acts 7:38
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Exo. 19.3, 17.

p Or Congregation; with the rest of the people in all their difficult Journey.

Gal. 3.19.

q See ver. 30. of this Chap.

x Gods Law and Word is so called, as the onely rule to walk by unto Life, Deut. 32.47. It is there said to be our life, and it is the onely ordinary means of a Spiritual and holy Life, which it begets and preserves.

entries.title: Acts 7:39
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
s Their glory being in their Fathers, St. Stephen minds them, that many of them rebelled against God, and his servant Moses; as they (their posterity) now were rebellious against Christ, who came to save them, as Moses before had done; but from a greater bondage, and by more valuable means.

t Not so much towards that Countrey, or food they had there, (Garlick and Onions) as towards their Idolatry and Superstition; a[illegible] in the following verse appears.

entries.title: Acts 7:40
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Exod. 32.1.

u According to the Egyptians, who held that there were many Gods, and divers degrees of Gods; they therefore speak in the plural number:

x Tho they confess the great deliverance wrought by Moses his means; yet how contemptibly do they speak of him.

y They could not but know that Moses was gone up into the Mount unto God, at his command, and had not forgotten them; but had left Aaron and Hur to govern them; yet they soon forgot both God and Moses, notwithstanding the large and late experience they had of his wonders; this is left upon record against them, Psal 106.13, 21.

entries.title: Acts 7:41
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
z In imitation of the Egyptians, who worshipped their God Apis in that, or the like form of an Ox.

a The Calf which they had made, which they could not be so sottish as to terminate their worship in, knowing that they themselves had made it, and it had not made them; yet they are for this charged to have committed Idolatry, 1 Cor. 10.6, 7.

b Which joy they express by feasting, singing, and dancing, Exod. 32.7.

c So, this Idol and Idols, generally are called, Psal. 115.4. and 135.15. which is enough to speak their emptiness and vanity; vain man can make but vain Gods.

entries.title: Acts 7:42
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d From being as a Father to them, to be a Judge over them, to punish them; whereas formerly he had blessed them.

e This was indeed to deliver them to Satan, God withholding his grace which they had abused, Rom. 1.24, 25. and giving them up, (to fall from one sin unto another) tho not positively, yet permissively.

f The Angels are so called, Luke 2.13. but it is rather here to be understood of the sun, moon, and stars, which are called so, Deut. 17.3. Isa. 40.26.

g The words here referred to, are in Amos 5 25. 'Tis said to be in the Book in the singular number, because the twelve small Prophets are by the Iews mentioned but as one Book.

h This positive question does vehemently deny, that they had offered any Sacrifices unto God, whilest they were in the wilderness; but at the same time they offered Sacrifices unto Idols; for when they had corrupted Gods worship, their Sacrifices were as no Sacrifices unto him, Isaiah 1.11. and 43.23.

entries.title: Acts 7:43
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
i On their shoulders, as they did the Ark.

k The Idol of the children of Ammon, which the Israelites were especially forbidden to worship, Lev. 18.21. and Lev. 20.2. yet they did ordinarily worship him, 2 Chron. 28.3. Ier. 7.3. And there was an high place built by Solomon for him, 1 Kings 11.7. The tabernacle of Molech, was either a chest or press in which that Idol was put, or the Chappels into which the worshippers of Molech were admitted; according to the quality of the Offering which they brought. Which of the planets they intended to honour hereby, whether the Sun, or Mars, or Saturn, it matters not so much; any of these, or any other of their Gods, might be called Molech, taking the word appellatively.

l Remphan in the place here cited, is called by the Prophet Chiun; which is one and the same Idol in both places, the Prophet calling it by its name then in use; and St. Stephen like unto the name the Septuagint had called it by; whither Saturn was intended by this, as some think, or Hercules as others, it is not our present business to enquire.

n Images and representatives of the hosts of Heaven, or of the Planets.

o The Prophet Amos saith, beyond Damascus, Amos 5.27. here St. Stephen does not contradict the Prophet, for they who were carryed away beyond Babylon, must needs be carryed away beyond Damascus, as the ten captive Tribes were, (unto whom this was threatned.)

entries.title: Acts 7:44
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
p Called also the Tabernacle of the congregation, Exod. 33.7. because about it on all solemn occasions the people assembled. Here 'tis called the Tabernacle of witness, because God here testified, or witnessed his glorious presence; and especially, because in it the Ark of the Covenant, the Law, and the Testimony were kept.

Or, Who spake.

q Exod. 25.40. Heb. 8.5. Moses was charged not to vary from the prescript; God being jealous of his own appointments: Now this is the rather spoken of by St. Stephen, that he might prove that the place where God was worshipped in, had varied, and therefore might also now be changed.

entries.title: Acts 7:45
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Josh. 3.14.

Or, Having received.

r Or Ioshua; it being the same name, as appears also, Heb. 4.8. onely Jesus is more according to the Greek use: Ioshua was a type of Jesus, and agreed with him in his name, and in the reason of his name; he having also saved the people, and brought them into the promised rest; yet the difference is as great between them, as betwixt the Heavenly Canaan, and the Earthly.

s They were not able to look upon an Israelite, whilest God was for them.

entries.title: Acts 7:46
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
1 Sam. 16.1. Chap. 13.22.

t As Luke 1.30.

u It was Davids earnest request, that he might any ways glorifie God, especially in his worship, and that he might know where the Ark should rest, and where the Temple was to be built, as Psalm 132. declares throughout.

entries.title: Acts 7:47
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
1 Chr. 17.[illegible].

x 1 Kings 6.10. 2 Chronicles 3.1, 2.

y A fixt and stable Structure, no[illegible] moveable, as the Tabernacle was.

entries.title: Acts 7:48
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
1 Kin. 8.27.

z This is also St. Pauls Doctrine, Chap. 17.24. which divers amongst the wiser Heathens were perswaded of; for God cannot be comprehended in any place, no, not where he is worshipped; and therefore they did foolishly conceive, that the worship of God was so tyed to the Temple, as if he himself had been included in it.

a The Primitive Christians abstained from calling the places of their assembling, by the name of Temples; and were charged by their Pagan-enemies for having no Altars, or Temples, or Images.

entries.title: Acts 7:49
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
b The place referred unto, is Isaiah 66.1.

Mat. 5.24. and 23.22.

c That shall be big enough for one so great as God is, 1 Kings 8.27.

entries.title: Acts 7:50
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
d As appears in the History of the Creation, Gen. 1.1.

e Spoken unto our capacity after the manner of men, and implies that God is too great to stand in need of Temples or Offerings; and that what worship he requires, is not for his own sake, for our righteousness cannot profit him; but for mans sake, that he might be exercised in the duties of Religion and devotion.

entries.title: Acts 7:51
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f A metaphor taken from heifers that are unaccustomed unto the yoke.

Exod. 32.9. Isa. 48.4.

g Such as had still depraved affections, which they ought to have put away rather than the foreskin of their flesh; for they were commanded to circumcise their hearts, Deut. 10.16. which also God promised to do for his people, [illegible] 30.6. And St. Paul was not the first who spake of a twofold circumcision, Rom. 2.28, 29. but God looked always to the inward and Spiritual part of his own Ordinances, and mens observance of them.

Lev. 26 41. Jer. 4.4. & 6.10. & 9.26.

h Such as were not so much as willing to hear, and know their duty.

i Speaking by his Prophets and Ministers, and exhorting to true and serious piety; by this St. Stephen would abate their glorying in circumcision, which they so much boasted of.

k Thus the Prophet Ezekiel, 16.44. unto which may be here alluded, as is the mother, so is the daughter.

entries.title: Acts 7:52
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l This is the rather said to stain all their glory from succession, and their Ancestors, Matth. 5.12. and 23.31, 37.

Chap. 3.14.

m Our Saviour deservedly, and by way of eminence is so called; as not onely being himself Iust, and fulfilling all righteousness; but being the Lord our righteousness, Ier. 23.6. and is of God made unto us, Wisdom, Righteousness, Sanctification, and Redemption, 1 Cor. 1.30. This word is used in a forensick sense, and is the same with innocent, and opposite to guilty; whereby St. Stephen vindicates our Saviour, notwithstanding the unjust sentence passed here upon him.

n In hiring Iudas.

o In that they excited Pilate to condemn him, and abetted the Soldiers and others, in executing of him.

entries.title: Acts 7:53
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Exod. 20.1.

p Or Ministery of Angels: The commandments were published from them Ministerially, or the Son of God, (called an Angel ver. 35.) accompanied with the Militia of Heaven, (for 'tis a Military Metaphor) did in the midst of that glorious retinue give the Law, Deut. 33.2. Psalm 68.8. Gal. 3.13, 19.

q They transgressed the Law, tho so gloriously delivered by Angels, and therefore it was no wonder if they despised the Gospel, that was published by so mean and contemptible Ministers.

entries.title: Acts 7:54
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
r They were angry to madness.

s Gnashing of teeth is the curse of the damned, Matthew 8.12. which men by their sins do prepare for; this corrasive was applyed by a skilful hand, would they have endured the cure.

See Chap. 5.33.

entries.title: Acts 7:55
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
t Filled with grace suitable to his present tryal and suffering.

u The glorious God, or so much of the Throne and glory of God, as Mortal eyes are capable for to see; being Iustified by God, tho condemned by Pilate:

x and standing ready to assist and comfort all that should suffer for his sake.

entries.title: Acts 7:56
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
y God not suffering any distance to hinder this refreshing sight.

Mat. 3.16.

z So Christ is frequently called; and St. Stephen would by this inform them, how vain they were in striving against Christ or his truth.

a As an Advocate, Soldier, or Captain for Stephen; or as one shewing the prize unto him, whic[illegible] he was now running for, and had need to be incouraged with the sight of: But it seems strange, that St. Stephen should tell the Iews of this Heavenly vision, being they did not see it, altho in the same place with him; but this he might do, 1. Out of his ardent love to Christ, desiring to magnifie him. 2. To invite his enemies to Repentance; now Heaven was opened, and Christs arms were stretched out to receive them. 3. To hinder any from being afraid to own Christ, and his truths. 4. To terrifie the most obdurate amongst them, by shewing them their judge, and minding them of his avenger. 5. That he might assert himself to be an eye-witness of Christs being risen again from the dead, which they made such difficulty to believe.

entries.title: Acts 7:57
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
b The rabble, or multitude.

c That they might show the great detestation of what was said, and might not contract any guilt from it.

d This violence and fury was both against the Law of God, and the Law of the Land; and the number of Zealots, (there were some amongst that people eminently so called) provoked the Romans to destroy both City and Temple.

entries.title: Acts 7:58
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
e That the City might not be polluted with his blasphemy.

1 Kin. 21.13. Luke 4.29.

f This punishment was appointed for such as seduced them to the worship of false Gods, Deut. 13.6, 10. and tho all power of Capital punishment was taken from them, as they themselves confess, Iohn 18.31. yet what will not popular rage attempt?

Chap. 22.20.

g Who were by the Law to cast the first stones, Deut. 17.7. whereby the witnesses, if they had not testified true, did take upon themselves the guilt of the blood that was spilt, and freed the people, who onely followed them in the Execution.

h Their upper garments, that they might carry, and cast down the heavier stones.

entries.title: Acts 7:59
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
i Stephen called upon him whom he saw standing, and that was our Saviour.

Psal. 31.5.

k Or my Soul; Thus our Saviour commended his Spirit into his Fathers hands, Luke 23.46. and this Disciple imitates his Master; and comforts himself with this, that to be sure his Soul should be safe, whatsoever became of his body.

entries.title: Acts 7:60
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
l A posture used in most earnest Prayers; and if so, he Prayed at least as earnestly for his enemies, as for himself; he praying for them kneeling, and for himself standing.

m Do not weigh it, reckon or impute it, that it may not remain against them, to hinder their Conversion; This our Saviour commanded, Matth. 5.44. this he practised, Luke 23.34. And whosoever can thus pray for his enemies, and do good for evil, hath a great evidence that the Spirit of Christ is in him.

n He dyed; his Death being thus expressed in that, 1. He dyed quietly, as one fallen into a sleep. 2. Because of his certain hope of the Resurrection. 3. As easily to be raised again by Christ, as one that sleeps is to be awaked by us. 4. It is an ordinary Hebraism to express Death by sleep; which made St. Luke use it amongst them, with whom it was frequently thus expressed.

entries.title: Acts 8:2
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
e It was an argument that they were devout (Religious) indeed, that they durst amongst such a multitude of persecutors, and furious Zealots, own their esteem for St. Stephen; It was piacular amongst the Iews, to touch the dead Corps of such an one as was put to Death for blasphemy; and these perform such Funeral rites for him, as were used for such onely as were of note and Eminency. As the Iews were wont to do at the Funeral, especially of Eminent persons; thus it was done at Iacobs Interment, Gen. 50. ult. and thus had been done more lately at Lazarus's Funeral, Iohn 11. even by our Saviour himself, ver. 3[illegible]. Which lamentation was the greater, because of the Churches loss at such a time.

Gen. 23.2. 2 Sam. 3.31.

entries.title: Acts 8:3
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
f Saul was a degree beyond the ordinary sort of persecutors, and was, as he does acknowledge of himself, eminently injurious, 1 Tim. 1.13.

Chap 22.4. & 26.10, 11. 1 Cor. 15.9. Gal. 1.13.

g House after house, sparing none.

h As by the hair of their heads.

i This to be sure, the Iews had yet retained power from the Romans to do: All this is but as a foil, to illustrate more the riches of Gods mercy towards Saul.

entries.title: Acts 8:4
entries.author: Continuation of Matthew Poole by various divines
entries.content:
Mat. 10.23. Chap. 11.19.

k Now the partition-wall was about to be broken down, and the Gentiles to be taken into the pale of the Church; God provides this strange means towards it.
